summary:
Lunar Navigator is a free, browser-based tool that helps mission planners, students and the public decide where and when to land on the Moon. Pick one of 17 landing sites or any point on the Moon and a date, and it shows in 3D where the Sun and Earth sit against the real horizon, built from NASA LRO elevation data. It reports hours of sunlight for solar power and hours of direct-to-Earth communication, and compares sites and dates side by side. That answers the challenge's core question: will this site have power and a link home on this date?

A Mission Designer adds the step before landing. Set the spacecraft's mass, engine and crew, drop a pin, and it finds every arrival opportunity, budgets fuel with the rocket equation, checks crew acceleration against NASA's Artemis limits and gives step-by-step burn guidance.

Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.034°, and 126 automated tests check the maths. At the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so a small change in site or date can decide a mission. Lunar Navigator makes that trade-off visible in seconds.
details:
Lunar Navigator is an interactive web application developed by Newguys Studios for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator. It helps users investigate whether a chosen lunar location will have sunlight and a clear view of Earth during a mission. Near the lunar south pole, low solar elevation means that surrounding terrain can create prolonged shadows. The project combines NASA datasets, scientific calculations and interactive visualizations to help students, space enthusiasts and teams exploring preliminary mission concepts compare landing sites, dates and spacecraft requirements.

Languages and technologies: The application uses HTML to structure its pages, CSS for styling and responsive layouts, and JavaScript, including ES modules, for calculations, controls and interactions. Its three-dimensional views use WebGL, with three.js supporting the Mission Designer’s lunar and terrain views. Node.js supports automated testing and an optional local server. The published application runs in a browser, allowing users to explore it without installing dedicated desktop software.

Features and creative approach: Users can select from 17 preset landing sites, enter coordinates or choose a location on a three-dimensional Moon. The Surface and Space interface combines terrain exploration, a drivable rover, time playback, horizon panoramas and comparison tables. Its creative approach connects visual exploration directly with analytical results: users can examine a location, compare conditions over time, plan a mission there and return to the surface at a selected arrival time. This shared location-and-time workflow makes abstract relationships between terrain, illumination and orbital timing easier to understand. A resource calculator also connects environmental conditions with ideal energy availability and data-transfer capacity.

Mission planning and factors considered: The Mission Designer considers spacecraft wet and dry mass, thrust, specific impulse, fuel reserves, starting orbit, target location, search radius and mission duration. It estimates velocity-change requirements, candidate arrival opportunities and burn sequences for landings, orbit transfers and inclination changes. Surface planning considers latitude, longitude, UTC date and time, terrain elevation, horizon obstruction, Sun and Earth elevation, sunlight duration and overlapping visibility windows. Resource estimates consider solar-panel output, battery capacity, power demand, data volume and downlink rate. Crewed scenarios additionally consider felt acceleration, exposure duration, crew posture and compression-garment selection. Checks distinguish pass, warning, fail, not checked and not applicable.

Scientific foundation and validation: The project uses NASA LRO LOLA elevation, LROC lunar imagery, NASA Blue Marble Earth imagery and astronomical formulas from Jean Meeus. Terrain sampling is approximately 500 metres around preset sites and 1.9 kilometres elsewhere, with distant horizon profiles extending to 400 kilometres. Cached JPL Horizons DE441 positions provide an astronomical reference. Project documentation reports a maximum directional difference of 0.036° across 4,326 cached hourly directions, alongside automated checks covering astronomy, arrival searches, fuel calculations and other functions.

Limitations and purpose: Lunar Navigator supports preliminary planning and education. Its two-body orbital model does not solve complete powered descent or terrain-safe landing, and coarse terrain can miss small obstacles. Earth visibility alone does not establish a communications link, while resource estimates simplify operational power and thermal behavior. Presenting these limits helps users compare possibilities and identify where detailed engineering analysis is required.
